Europe’s IF24 Hydrogen Auction Selected Projects, Not Yet a Market

The visible story from Europe’s second renewable-hydrogen auction is severe attrition. Sixty-one bids entered. Fifteen projects were initially invited to prepare grant agreements. By January 2026, only six had signed, representing 381.25 MW of electrolyser capacity and €270.6 million of support.

By Bottleneck Briefs · Published 2026-07-24 · 14 min read

In brief

  • €270.6 million | six IF24 grant agreements signed in January 2026.
  • 381.25 MW | final capacity, versus 2,336.96 MW initially selected.
  • 8% | completion security screens sponsor commitment before grant signature.
  • Qualification | the cohort has not demonstrated repeatable procurement or operation.
  • July 2027 | the first meaningful test is exact-scope financial close.

Key figures

61bids submitted to the second EU hydrogen auction
15projects initially invited to prepare grant agreements
6projects that ultimately signed
381.25 MWsigned electrolyser capacity
€270.6Mmaximum support across the signed cohort

The auction selected a contracting problem

Official results graphic or table

Official final cohort: six signed projects, 381.25 MW and bids from €0.33/kg to €1.88/kg.

Open source visual from European Commission

Reuse: license unclear - rights not verified · Attribution: European Commission, DG CLIMA

The final cohort retained roughly 16% of the capacity represented by the original fifteen selections. The simplest explanation is that developers bid too aggressively. That is partly right, but it misses the more useful commercial lesson.

IF24 did not merely rank hydrogen producers by subsidy request. It forced each selected developer to move through a sequence:

auction qualification → completion security → grant signature → binding contracts → sponsor and lender approval → financial close → operation → verified production → premium payment.

Official news lead image

Open source visual from CINEA

The fixed premium addresses one part of future revenue. It does not fund construction upfront, set the wholesale electricity price, secure a grid connection, order an electrolyser, appoint an EPC contractor, create a pipeline or compel a customer to sign a long-term purchase agreement. Payments begin only after eligible hydrogen is produced and verified. (IF24 call terms)

That makes the completion guarantee a sequential qualification gate, not the final economic constraint. Developers that accept it demonstrate that they will bear its cost, allocate collateral or credit capacity, and accept fixed milestones. Only then does the harder package become visible: qualifying power, binding demand, equipment, construction risk, permits, equity and finance.

Six projects cleared the same gate by different routes

The signed projects should not be treated as a homogeneous portfolio. Their capacities, customers, products and sponsor structures differ sharply.

Project figures come from the European Commission and CINEA’s January 2026 award records. (signed IF24 cohort)

Kristinestad PtX is the largest. Koppö Energia’s current design combines 200 MW of electrolysis with an e-methanol plant targeting about 450 tonnes per day. Thyssenkrupp Uhde has performed front-end engineering for the methanol process, following earlier engineering work involving ANDRITZ. The chain extends beyond electrolysis into biogenic carbon dioxide, transport, synthesis and product sales. (Kristinestad FEED)

Its environmental record also illustrates why development status must be dated carefully. A regional authority previously required supplementation to an environmental assessment, but that work was completed and a reasoned conclusion followed in March 2025. The remaining questions concern the current configuration, final permits, customers, procurement and finance—not the obsolete supplementation request.

NOON presents a different route. Iberdrola reports a 120 MW project, 161,000 tonnes of planned hydrogen production over ten years and a grant of about €135.5 million. An integrated utility can supply renewable electricity from its own portfolio, carry development expenditure on its balance sheet and manage customer relationships across existing businesses. That may remove interfaces that burden a stand-alone project company. It still does not establish that NOON has completed its final offtake, EPC and investment package. (NOON project)

H2CRI is smaller at 30 MW and bid €0.44 per kilogram. Saeta Yield describes dedicated or nearby renewable resources and intended sales into industrial and heavy-transport markets. The public evidence establishes the concept and the grant, but not the commercial terms that would make those customers financeable. (H2CRI)

GH2Move-VLC is smaller again at 5 MW. Public project descriptions present a compact mobility model built around renewable power, compressed hydrogen and logistics demand near Valencia. Those details are useful, but the underlying customer and procurement contracts remain insufficiently transparent to treat the project as a proven template for distributed hydrogen deployment.

Rjukan shows why public milestones need exact scope

Rjukan is the strongest apparent exception to the cohort’s qualification status.

Norwegian Hydrogen has announced an investment decision and reports permits, reserved grid capacity, a power agreement and financing support. Worley Rosenberg has carried out FEED work and described an exclusive EPC option, a liquid-hydrogen facility and a target of initial deliveries during 2028. (Rjukan investment decision)

Those are stronger signals than a grant, memorandum or concept study. They suggest that Rjukan may already be moving toward early deployment.

The complication is scope. The IF24 award table lists 18.75 MW. Worley has described a 25 MW facility, while another public project description has referred to a larger FEED scope. The relationship among the 18.75 MW award and larger public project descriptions remains unresolved.

Until the grant annex, permits, financing and EPC package are reconciled, Rjukan cannot serve as a clean demonstration that the exact IF24 action has reached formal financial close. It does, however, expose a limitation in public-document analysis: a corporate-financed project can advance through investment approval, permits and procurement without issuing a conventional “project finance closed” announcement.

That distinction matters for the forecast. Public announcement counts may understate real conversion. The correct test is not whether a project uses the phrase financial close. It is whether the precise grant-supported asset has committed capital, an executable construction package and binding demand.

The guarantee exposes the next gate

The completion guarantee equals 8% of the project’s maximum requested grant. It must use the prescribed form and come from a qualifying financial institution or eligible insurer. A blocked cash account is not accepted as a substitute. The sponsor bears the cost.

The instrument may be called if the project fails to reach financial close, enter operation, deliver planned capacity or retain its grant before operation. At the signed cohort’s aggregate award value, 8% corresponds to roughly €21.65 million of maximum face exposure.

That is meaningful as a commitment test, but it should not be confused with the capital required to build 381.25 MW of electrolysis and its associated power, water, compression, liquefaction, storage, synthesis and transport systems. Nor is the face amount a revenue pool for banks or insurers. Their economics lie in undisclosed fees, collateral, recourse and credit usage.

Financial close imposes the more revealing test. Projects must provide signed power-sourcing arrangements, hydrogen or derivative offtake, an electrolyser purchase contract, final investment approval, financing documentation, an EPC contract and an updated financial model. Maritime projects must support at least 60% of planned production with qualifying arrangements.

The guarantee therefore does not replace financeability. It causes developers to confront it earlier.

The projects that left identify the deeper constraints

The withdrawal cases show why completion security cannot be the sole explanation.

H2-Hub Lubmin left amid uncertainty linked to delayed German implementation of revised renewable-energy rules, according to reporting that cited the developer. The problem was not simply access to a guarantee. Regulatory uncertainty affected whether the hydrogen could qualify and whether customers would sign durable contracts.

Zeevonk provides an even cleaner physical case. The 560 MW auction configuration depended on the Delta Rhine Corridor. When the expected corridor schedule moved from 2028 to 2032, the project’s accessible market and original timetable deteriorated. A production premium could not restore a delayed transport route. (Dutch corridor record)

Gen2-LH2 shows that withdrawal need not mean permanent abandonment. Its IF24 configuration was 82.21 MW at €0.59 per kilogram. In the next auction cycle, an official IF25 list included a 12 MW proposal at €3.48 per kilogram. The comparison suggests redesign and repricing, although the underlying technical scopes may differ. (IF25 auction)

Hammerfest supplies the strongest negative control within the signed cohort. GreenH still describes the project as early-stage and says construction can proceed once buyers are secured. Potential coastal and offshore customers do not yet amount to demonstrated bankable demand. (HammerfestH2)

These cases narrow the thesis. Completion security is a real screen, but demand, regulation and shared infrastructure can dominate the outcome. The guarantee does not solve those constraints; it reveals whether a sponsor is prepared to keep carrying them.

Who controls the transition

CINEA controls grant administration, milestone acceptance and premium payment. The guarantee issuer controls access to acceptable completion security. Sponsors decide whether to commit equity and corporate credit. Lenders and technical advisers determine whether construction, customer and downside risks are acceptable.

Power suppliers and grid operators control the cost and legal quality of RFNBO-compliant electricity. Electrolyser manufacturers control delivery slots, warranties and performance. EPC contractors control integration, schedule and interface risk. Customers control whether projected revenue becomes a binding obligation.

After commissioning, control moves again. Certifiers, meters and production-data systems determine whether hydrogen qualifies for the premium. Liquefaction, compression, storage, trucking, refuelling and port operators determine whether it reaches the buyer.

This creates several potential spend paths: guarantee and financing fees, EPC and equipment procurement, renewable-power contracting, hydrogen conditioning, logistics, certification and maintenance. But required activity is not the same as durable value capture.

Worley may convert Rjukan FEED into EPC revenue. Thyssenkrupp Uhde may expand its role at Kristinestad. ANDRITZ and HydrogenPro have earlier exposure to the Finnish development chain. Iberdrola may retain power, project integration and customer value within its own platform. These are exposures to the transition, not evidence of booked revenue or investment merit.

Where value may move—and where it may stay

If projects advance, spending moves from grant preparation and early engineering toward construction, equipment, power and physical delivery. Once plants operate, some expenditure becomes recurring: electricity, certification, balancing, maintenance, storage and transport.

The strongest potential control points are not necessarily the largest capital items. An EPC contractor may receive a large one-time contract but have limited long-term leverage. A certifier may receive a smaller recurring fee while controlling evidence required for payment. An integrated utility may retain customer ownership, power margin and financing control without exposing each component as external revenue.

Double counting is a major risk. The €270.6 million grant is not present supplier revenue. The €21.65 million guarantee face amount is not an issuer fee pool. Electrolyser packages may already sit inside EPC values. Hydrogen sales and fixed-premium payments support the same kilograms and should not be counted as separate demand volumes.

The same caution applies to software. RFNBO rules require auditable links among renewable generation, time matching, electrolyser consumption and hydrogen output. That creates a workflow need, particularly as hourly matching becomes the default in 2030. It does not yet prove that a concentrated, high-margin software market will form. No named cohort-level platform, certifier or metering architecture has been disclosed.

The counterargument is stronger than “projects take time”

The strongest case against this column is that the guarantee may be administratively important but economically secondary.

Rjukan may already have advanced beyond qualification through corporate or public financing. Integrated sponsors such as Iberdrola may close projects without public lender syndicates. Confidential contracts may make the public record look less mature than the projects are. If so, grant signature could be a stronger predictor of construction than the current evidence suggests.

The closest historical comparison also leans more positive than a simple attrition narrative. In the first European Hydrogen Bank auction, seven projects were selected, six signed grant agreements in 2024 and CINEA described five as being in implementation by January 2026. “Implementation” does not establish financial close, construction completion or certified production.

What is similar is the sequence from production-linked support to grant implementation. What is different is IF24’s larger initial cohort, maritime category, explicit completion-security requirement and much greater pre-signature withdrawal.

The thesis survives, but in narrower form. The evidence supports “grant signature is not financial close.” It does not support “the guarantee is the principal cause of project conversion or failure.” The guarantee is better understood as the device that forces the deeper commercial package into view.

The next state transition has a date

The cohort is currently best classified as qualification. Moving to early deployment requires more than additional partnerships or FEED announcements.

The evidence should connect the exact IF24-supported scope to final investment approval, unconditional EPC execution, equipment procurement, binding offtake, permits and committed capital. One project reaching that standard would demonstrate conversion. Several projects repeating it would demonstrate a procurement pattern.

The first useful settlement point is July 20, 2027. By then, one or more projects should have produced exact-scope FID or financial-close evidence if the signed cohort is converting at pace. Four or more compliant closes would materially weaken the qualification thesis. Zero would suggest that the premium and security screen selected projects that still could not assemble the downstream package.

The formal programme test comes later, approximately 2.5 years after each project’s grant signature. Exact signature dates and CINEA milestone records will be needed to settle that test cleanly.

What to watch

  • By July 20, 2027, at least one project confirms exact-scope FID or financial close.
  • By July 20, 2027, four compliant closes would overturn the selective-conversion view.
  • Rjukan publishes an EPC commitment tied explicitly to the 18.75 MW IF24 action.
  • Hammerfest signs a binding maritime customer before announcing construction commitment.
  • CINEA publishes project-level financial-close dates for the six signed grants.
